vignette:
Jacob is 21 years old, though if you saw him hunched over the steering wheel of his city bus, you might guess older. He is tall but carries himself as if trying to take up less space. He lives alone in a small apartment near the depot. He has been driving the number 7 route for eight months-steady work, no passengers complaining, just the same loop through the industrial district and back. He prefers the early shift, when the streets are quiet and the interior lights of the bus are still dim.

Two years ago, Jacob was not a bus driver. He was a gunner in an armored vehicle, rolling through a dusty province in a war he barely understood. He had enlisted at 18, right out of high school, because he didn't know what else to do and because his father said it would make a man out of him. For six months, the deployment was boring and hot and heavy with the smell of diesel. Then the IED hit. He remembers the sound-not a boom, but a stopped silence that lasted a fraction of a second before the world folded in on itself. He remembers the hot wetness on his face, and the screaming of his driver, and the way the blood pooled under his own legs. He does not remember being pulled out. He remembers the hospital, the morphine, the letters from home he could not read.

He was medically discharged, honorably, with a clean set of X-rays and a scar across his left shin. The physical wounds healed. But the bus is where the past keeps finding him.

A backfire from a pickup truck makes him flinch so hard he accidentally pushes the brake pedal and throws a standing passenger forward. He apologizes through the intercom, voice flat, but inside his chest is a wild rabbit. Construction sites with jackhammers send him into a cold sweat. Every time the bus passes under a low bridge, he ducks involuntarily, expecting the crack of metal on concrete. He avoids broken glass on the road. He avoids the highway, where the median looks like a berm that could hide anything.

At night, Jacob does not sleep. He lies on his back, eyes open, listening to the hum of the refrigerator, which sounds like a generator. He runs through the pre-check of the bus in his mind-mirrors, air brakes, tires-because counting distracts him from the images that want to replay. The worst ones are the faces. He did not know the driver's real name. He only knew his first name, Tommy. Tommy's face after the blast is the one that visits Jacob most: eyes open, mouth half-open, a thin line of blood from one ear. Jacob did not die, but something in him stopped working that day.

He does not talk about the deployment. When his mother asks, he says, "It was fine." When his supervisor notices the flinching and suggests he take a day off, Jacob says, "I'm good." He has no friends from the service; he deleted their numbers because group texts about barbecues felt like a lie. He does not seek out other veterans. At the VA clinic, he filled out a PCL-5 once for a routine visit, scored a 53, and stuffed the paper in his pocket without asking what it meant.

Driving is the only thing that makes sense. The route is predictable. He knows every crack in the pavement. He knows which stop has a man who always smells of beer, and which turn requires a slow-down because of the dip. He can control the speed, the door, the lights. He cannot control the sudden surge of rage that comes when a car cuts him off-his hands go white on the steering wheel, and he has to count to ten to keep from shouting over the intercom.

Last week, a passenger dropped a metal water bottle. The sound was sharp and loud. Jacob slammed on the brakes, threw the bus into park, and sat trembling for a full thirty seconds while passengers stared. He managed to say, "Sorry, thought I saw something." He drove the rest of the route in a fog, then sat in the depot parking lot afterward, engine off, gripping the wheel until his fingers ached. He does not know why he feels safer inside the bus than anywhere else. He only knows that outside it, the world feels too open, too full of sudden noises he cannot brace for.
